name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,717

clue.text: Tangled cable ties? We won't have it!

definitions.note: a sentence spoken by the people, standing for the plural noun

indicators.note: tangled things are knotted and out of order, so the letters must be rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written: nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to put up with a knotted mess of cable ties.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a whole exclamation: CELIBATES are people who say 'we won't have it', where 'it' is the slang sense of sex.
explanation.definitionFit: People who abstain from sexual relations could say they refuse to have 'it', a coy euphemism for intercourse.

clue.text: Pal I chat up (keeping under wraps old sausage)

indicators.note: things that are up in the air or all churned up are disordered, so the letters get mixed
to keep something under wraps is to hide it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: taken as written: eight letters to rearrange
O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: Someone talks up a friend while keeping quiet about an old sausage.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearrange PAL I CHAT to CHIPLATA, then tuck O inside to make CHIPOLATA.
explanation.definitionFit: A chipolata is a small thin pork link, a specific kind of the general meat product named.

clue.text: Temp crazy American cut? I don't know what to say!

indicators.note: a cut word has been trimmed, so its final letter is lopped off

blocks.note: LOCO is American slang for crazy; trimmed of its last letter

blocks.clueFragment: I don't know what to say!
blocks.note: the hesitant noise of someone lost for words

explanation.surface: Someone is lost for words about a mad American temporary worker who has been sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' looks like a sacking in the story but only trims a letter. LOCO is American slang, hence 'American'.
explanation.definitionFit: A locum is a doctor or professional standing in for an absent colleague, a stand-in worker on short contract.

clue.text: Fairly clever Brits high on drugs

indicators.note: someone on drugs is scrambled and disordered, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written: nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A sneer that British people are only smart when they are stoned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High on drugs' reads as one phrase, but 'high' belongs to the letters to shuffle and 'on drugs' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Bright means intelligent and the suffix -ish softens it to somewhat, giving moderately smart.

clue.text: Old man in article on several Tory leaders' history?

indicators.note: leaders go at the front, so only the opening letters of the words are kept
in a down clue one piece sitting on another is placed above it
being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece is put within another

blocks.note: the definite article
pa is an informal word for father
first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A dad writes a piece on the history of several Conservative leaders.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down light the article sits on top of the initials, and the father slots in between. The question mark flags that history is only one way to describe it.
explanation.definitionFit: Bygone times collectively are what history studies, so the phrase is a fair if loose equivalent.

clue.text: Women who nurse women with habits?

blocks.note: first meaning: senior hospital nurses, a British rank
second meaning: nuns, who wear the robe called a habit

explanation.walkthrough: 'Habits' suggests vices; it is the religious garment. In Britain a sister is a senior ward nurse.
explanation.definitionFit: The title applies both to senior female hospital nurses and to members of religious orders such as nuns.

clue.text: What a vampire does is no good at all

blocks.note: first meaning: draws blood from its victim
second meaning: slang for being terrible

explanation.walkthrough: Both parts are verb phrases in the third person, matching the one word in two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers a vampire drawing blood by mouth and, as slang, something being awful or worthless.

clue.text: Southern tough injecting MDMA and horse

indicators.note: to inject is to put something inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for southern
a Ted, short for Teddy boy, is a 1950s British tearaway
MDMA is the drug ecstasy, known as E

explanation.surface: A southern thug shoots up ecstasy, and horse too, a slang name for heroin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horse' looks like more drugs (heroin), but it is the definition. TED takes E inside after S.
explanation.definitionFit: A steed is a literary or poetic name for a riding mount, synonymous with the animal.

clue.text: Banknotes possibly overlooked by Tory candidate

indicators.note: in a down clue something overlooked has another piece standing above it

blocks.note: Con is short for Conservative
banknotes are legal tender; 'possibly' marks an example

explanation.surface: A Conservative candidate keeps an eye on the money.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue the party abbreviation stands above the money word. Legal tender is money that must be accepted in payment.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone standing for election or competing for a prize is a rival in the running, a synonym.

clue.text: Way to save family without any money

indicators.note: to save something is to keep it safe within, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
kin are relatives

explanation.surface: Advice on how to rescue a household that has run out of cash.
explanation.walkthrough: ST holds KIN. Skint is everyday British slang for broke.
explanation.definitionFit: Skint is informal British slang meaning penniless or broke, completely out of cash.

clue.text: Blundering in chess? It's an irritating feeling!

indicators.note: blundering means making clumsy mistakes, so the letters fall out of order

blocks.note: taken as written: nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Making mistakes at chess is annoying.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark breaks the sentence, but 'It' still belongs to the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Itchiness is the prickly sensation on the skin that makes one want to scratch, an irritation.

clue.text: General weariness is some rotten nuisance

indicators.note: some of something is only a part of it, so the letters lie within the words

blocks.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: Feeling fed up is a horrible nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: Read through rotTEN NUIsance.
explanation.definitionFit: Ennui is a French borrowing for listless boredom and dissatisfaction, an all-round lack of interest.

clue.text: Ohio politician enthralled by my sex appeal

indicators.note: to be enthralled is to be held captive, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: O is an old abbreviation for the US state
both are exclamations of surprise
Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: An Ohio politician is captivated by the speaker's attractiveness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' is not a possessive here but an exclamation of surprise, like 'my goodness!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Oomph is informal for vigour or physical attractiveness, the quality of being alluring and sexy.

clue.text: A pair of guys going over Dutch tenor's revision

indicators.note: each going in front of the next item, so the pieces line up one before another

blocks.note: taken as written
the first of the two men
D is the abbreviation for Dutch
the second of the two men
T is the abbreviation for tenor

explanation.surface: Two men check a Dutch tenor's corrections to a score.
explanation.walkthrough: The pair gives MEN twice: one goes before D, the other before T.
explanation.definitionFit: An amendment is a change or correction made to a text, the same idea as a reworking.

clue.text: Fix a drink infused with pop mostly

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
what is infused is steeped inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: taken as written
a pint of beer
the word trimmed of its last letter

explanation.surface: Mix a drink with a splash of fizzy soda.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fix a drink' looks like bartending, but 'Fix' alone is the definition, and the drink is a glass of beer.
explanation.definitionFit: To fix a date or time is to settle or set it, which is one sense of appoint.

clue.text: Soldier on horse of the greatest importance

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece sitting on another is placed above it

blocks.note: a para is a paratrooper
a mount is a horse for riding

explanation.surface: A cavalryman on horseback is crucially important.
explanation.walkthrough: A para is a paratrooper, a parachute soldier, so the surface's cavalryman is a misleading picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Paramount means supreme or foremost, above everything else in rank and significance.

clue.text: 60s youth singers making a comeback for fame

indicators.note: a comeback goes back the way it came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a mod was a member of a 1960s British youth subculture
informers who sing to the police are rats

explanation.surface: A sixties pop group reforms to chase celebrity again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singers' suggests a band, but here it means informers, since to sing is slang for telling tales.
explanation.definitionFit: Stardom is the state of being a celebrity, widely known and admired, which is fame.

clue.text: Lad tunes out, having inhaled good hallucinogen

indicators.note: out can mean wild or out of place, so the letters are rearranged
what is inhaled is taken inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: taken as written: eight letters to rearrange
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A young man zones out after breathing in something mind-altering.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearrange LAD TUNES and slip G inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Angel dust is street slang for PCP, a drug that causes visions and altered perception.

clue.text: Gives drugs to Hoskins and group on LSD coming up

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece sitting on another is placed above it
in a down light coming up means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: Hoskins is the setter, who refers to themself
a set is a group
acid is slang for LSD

explanation.surface: The setter and friends are tripping, doling out drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's name stands for ME. SET above ACID is read upwards as DICATES.
explanation.definitionFit: To medicate someone is to administer medicine or treatment, supplying pharmaceuticals.

clue.text: Supporter punches a poor player in Lincoln?

indicators.note: a punch drives into something, so one piece is driven inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
a bra is a supporting undergarment
a ham is a bad, overacting actor

explanation.surface: A fan hits a weak footballer at Lincoln, a city with an English football club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporter' suggests a fan; it is an undergarment. 'Poor player' is a bad actor, not a sportsman.
explanation.definitionFit: Abraham Lincoln was the sixteenth US president; the question mark flags that the surname alone points to his first name.

clue.text: Macho fellow I caught exerting bad influence

blocks.note: macho means manly
F is the abbreviation for fellow
taken as written
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A tough guy is arrested for leading others astray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught' suggests an arrest, but it is the cricket abbreviation C.
explanation.definitionFit: Malefic is a literary or astrological word for causing harm or evil, a baleful power.

clue.text: Drunk on beer, royal knocked over editor

indicators.note: something knocked over is upended, so its letters run backwards

blocks.note: regal means royal
ED is the abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: A tipsy royal topples a newspaper editor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk on beer' looks like part of the story but is the definition; the wordplay never mentions beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lagered is British slang for intoxicated, specifically from too much pale fizzy ale.

clue.text: Reveal what a sunbathing nudist might do?

definitions.text: what a sunbathing nudist might do?
definitions.note: the phrase describes an action, matched by the verb phrase

blocks.note: first meaning: expose or uncover

blocks.clueFragment: what a sunbathing nudist might do?
blocks.note: second meaning, playfully literal: stretch out naked

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading takes the idiom literally, with 'lay' in the colloquial sense of lie; the question mark flags the liberty.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to expose or disclose something hidden, while literally it pictures reclining unclothed.

clue.text: Firm friend describing male in charge in a funny way

indicators.note: to describe a circle is to draw round, so one piece goes around another

blocks.note: CO is the abbreviation for company
an ally is a friend
M is the abbreviation for male
IC is the abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: A loyal friend talks about the boss in a jokey manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm friend' reads as a loyal pal, but it splits into a company abbreviation and a friend, which wrap round the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Comically means amusingly or humorously, an adverb for something that provokes laughter.

clue.text: Republican dons ready for economic collapse

indicators.note: to don clothing is to put it on, so one piece is wrapped around another

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for Republican
ready money, or 'the readies', is cash

explanation.surface: A Republican gets dressed and braces for a market meltdown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dons' looks like academics; here CASH dons R. Readies is British slang for cash.
explanation.definitionFit: A crash is a sudden severe fall in markets or the wider financial system.

clue.text: Vulgar bloke pinching primate's bottom

indicators.note: the bottom of a word is its end, so only the final letter is kept
to pinch something is to grip it, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: a chap is a man
final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A crude man pinches an ape's backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinching' and 'bottom' look like a groping scene; they are a container and a final-letter selection.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheap can mean tacky or in poor taste, a coarse lack of refinement.

clue.text: Ring back around lunchtime to get Plant

indicators.note: to go around something is to enclose it, so one piece sits within another
going back means running the other way, so the letters read in reverse

blocks.note: to ring is to phone, make a call
one o'clock, written as the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A garden centre is told to phone back at lunch about a plant.
explanation.walkthrough: Lunchtime is taken as one o'clock, so I. CALL wraps I to make CALIL, then turns round.
explanation.definitionFit: Lilac is a flowering shrub with fragrant purple or white blooms, an example of vegetation.

clue.text: Story and books written about Navy Command?

indicators.note: about can mean turned around, so these letters are written the other way

blocks.note: a lie is a made-up story
OT is the Old Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: A tale and some books are written about naval leadership.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Navy Command' looks like a headquarters; the question mark marks it as an order shouted at sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Lie to is a sailing order to bring a ship nearly to a halt facing the wind, so an instruction afloat.

clue.text: Coach in hospital unit gets poor treatment

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece is put within another

blocks.note: A&E, accident and emergency, is the British name for a hospital emergency room
a coach is a long-distance bus

explanation.surface: A sports coach in casualty is badly treated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coach' suggests a trainer; it is the vehicle. The ampersand of A&E is ignored, leaving A and E around BUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Abuse is cruel or harmful handling of a person, mistreatment or ill use.

clue.text: High-rise domicile you permitted use of is windy

blocks.note: a flat is an apartment
text-speak spelling
to lend is to let someone use something

explanation.surface: The tower-block apartment you let someone borrow is draughty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Windy' seems to describe the high flat, but it means suffering from wind in the gut.
explanation.definitionFit: Flatulent means affected by intestinal gas, which in British slang is being windy.

clue.text: Become more active after plonk is brought round by head office

indicators.note: bringing something round turns it to face the other way, so its letters run backwards
coming after means following, so one piece is placed behind another

blocks.note: HO is the abbreviation for head office
to plonk something down is to put it

explanation.surface: Things liven up once head office hands round the cheap wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plonk' looks like cheap wine, a common British word, but here it is the verb to put down.
explanation.definitionFit: To hot up is British idiom for getting livelier or more intense, as a contest does.

clue.text: Unusual reactions for crosswords, perhaps

indicators.note: something unusual departs from the normal order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written: nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Solvers have odd responses to puzzles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' marks crosswords as one example of what a setter makes.
explanation.definitionFit: A crossword is a thing a setter has made up, one example of an invented work.
